title: Utility Types & Type-Level Tools
objective: After this lesson you will be able to reach for the right built-in utility type when refactoring (Partial, Required, Pick, Omit, Record, ReturnType, Awaited…), and understand keyof, indexed access and typeof as the operators they're built from.
why: Real codebases are full of derived shapes: an update PATCH that sends some fields, a list view that shows three columns, a table keyed by ID, a handler wrapping a function's return. Writing those by hand duplicates the source type and rots on every model change. Utility types transform existing types programmatically — the refactoring superpower that keeps one source of truth.

blocks.text: Three tiny operators power every utility type. Learn them once and the whole toolbox becomes readable:

`typeof` in a type position is the quiet hero: it means your *runtime* constants can be the single source of truth their types derive from. Change the value, and every dependent type updates on the next compile. The `keyof` + indexed-access pair is how the compiler can follow a property name to its type — you used this in Lesson 6's `prop<T, K extends keyof T>`.

blocks.title: The mental model
blocks.text: Think of these as array methods for types: keyof is Object.keys (as a type union), T[K] is indexing into a lookup table, and typeof x is "the type of this actual value." Everything else in this lesson is a function built from these primitives.
These six cover the overwhelming majority of real-world shape derivations. Each entry shows the operator definition (right) so it demystifies, plus the canonical use case:

rows: A keyed lookup with known keys
Type of what a function returns
Follows the function when it changes

blocks.text: Two details to internalize. First, these compose — a real pattern is a paginated list view: `type UserListItem = Pick<User, "email" | "role">` then `type UserList = { items: UserListItem[]; total: number }`. Second, they're *lazy*: `Partial<User>` re-derives from `User` on every compile, so adding a field to User flows into every derived type automatically. That's the single-source-of-truth payoff.
One modern addition earns its own headline because async code is everywhere. `Awaited<T>` unwraps a promise's type — including recursively through nested promises:
A refactoring story (how it appears in real applications)

blocks.title: Common mistake #6
blocks.text: Omitting a field for security with `Omit<User, "passwordHash">` and believing the field is gone at runtime. Utility types are type-level transforms — the actual object still carries the property. The pattern is correct as a *contract* (you can't accidentally access it through the typed view), but the strip must happen in code: `const { passwordHash, ...safe } = user; return safe satisfies Omit<User, "passwordHash">;`

items: keyof, indexed access T[K], and typeof are the operators; every utility type is a function over them
Partial = update payloads, Pick/Omit = verified views, Record = exhaustive dictionaries, ReturnType/Awaited = function-derived types
Utility types re-derive on every compile — one source of truth, zero manual syncing across derived shapes
typeof + a runtime constant makes the value the single source of truth for its whole type family
Type-level removal (Omit) doesn't remove runtime properties — pair it with a destructure for real stripping

exercise.prompt: You're hardening an API layer. Given `interface User { readonly id: number; email: string; passwordHash: string; role: "admin" | "user"; displayName?: string }`, define: (1) `PublicUser` — everything a client may see, i.e. User minus passwordHash; (2) `UserPatch` — the update payload, any subset of email/role/displayName; (3) a `sanitize(user: User): PublicUser` function that actually strips the secret at runtime (no type lies); and (4) a `RolePerms` record mapping every role to its allowed permissions list, exhaustive by construction.
hints: PublicUser is one Omit away; UserPatch is a Partial over a Pick.
For sanitize, destructure the secret out: const { passwordHash, ...rest } = user; — then return rest. The spread genuinely removes the field at runtime.
The `satisfies` operator (TS 4.9+) lets you check the destructure's type against PublicUser without widening: return rest satisfies PublicUser.
RolePerms: Record<User["role"], string[]> — indexed access pulls the role union so the record stays exhaustive if roles grow.
exercise.why: Each piece derives from User, so the source of truth is singular: add displayName and every derived type updates; add a role and RolePerms refuses to compile until permissions are decided. The sanitize function is the honest pairing — a type-level Omit claims the field is unreachable through the view, while the destructure+satisfies actually removes it from the object. This layering (contract derived from the model, runtime behavior matching the contract) is exactly how production API layers stay safe as models evolve.

quiz.q: type Draft = Partial<User> — what is Draft["email"]?
quiz.explain: Partial maps every property to optional, so each access yields T | undefined. Callers get subset freedom; consumers of the draft handle absence — that trade is the point of the utility.

quiz.q: You need a type for exactly { email: string; role: "admin" | "user" } derived from User. Which is most direct?
quiz.explain: Pick keeps the listed properties — a positive selection matching the requirement exactly. Omit also works but listing what to remove gets longer and drifts as User grows. Choose by which list is shorter and more stable.

quiz.q: type Perms = Record<"read" | "write", boolean> — what must an object of this type contain?
options: Either a read or a write key
Exactly both read and write keys, each boolean — missing either is a compile error
Any string keys with boolean values
quiz.explain: Record over a literal union demands every key. That exhaustiveness (plus autocomplete for the keys) is why Record beats a hand-written interface for mappings between known sets.

quiz.q: const endpoints = { users: "/users", orders: "/orders" } as const; — what does keyof typeof endpoints give you?
options: "users" | "orders" — the literal keys, perfect for routing lookups
quiz.explain: typeof captures the object's shape; as const locks the values AND keys as literal types. keyof then yields exactly "users" | "orders" — a routing table that's both the runtime data and the compile-time key union, one source of truth.
Awaited strips the promise wrapper one level (handling nested promises recursively): Promise<User[]> → User[]. It's how generic wrappers normalize async results without knowing the payload type.

summary: keyof, indexed access and typeof are the primitives; Partial, Pick, Omit, Record, ReturnType and Awaited are the everyday functions built on them. Derived types re-compute on every compile, so models stay the single source of truth and views can't drift. Pair type-level removal with runtime destructuring when data must actually disappear, and let Record over literal unions enforce exhaustiveness.
